have_openmx <- requireNamespace("OpenMx", quietly = TRUE)

## Studying associations among individual growth parameters

Suppose researchers measure two processes repeatedly, such as well-being
and stress, and want to know whether people who change more quickly in one
process also change more quickly in the other. A mixed model can estimate
each person's intercept and slope, but those estimates contain error.
Simply correlating the estimated random effects treats them as perfectly
measured and can bias the associations.

This vignette uses 2S-PA to account for measurement error in empirical Bayes
(EB) estimates of random effects. We fit a separate mixed model for each
process in stage 1, then estimate the covariances among their random
intercepts and slopes in stage 2. The simulated processes have different
measurement schedules: five occasions for one and twenty for the other.
This lets us analyze their associations without fitting a single
multivariate growth model.

Stage 2 uses `tspa_mx_model()` to retain each person's measurement
information. These examples require `OpenMx` and are skipped if it is not
installed. For methodological background, see Lai and Liu (2026).

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(R2spa)
library(lme4)
if (have_openmx) library(OpenMx)
```

`get_fs()` returns one row per person for these models. The latent random
intercept `u0` is measured by the score `fs_u0`, and the latent random
slope `u1` by `fs_u1`. Their score loadings and error covariances can vary
with the number and timing of observations. OpenMx uses definition variables
to fix these quantities to each person's values.

The helper below extracts the estimated latent covariance matrix from the
OpenMx fit for the comparisons later in the vignette.

```{r}
lat_cov <- function(fit, lat) {
  v <- c(fit$manifestVars, fit$latentVars)
  idx <- match(lat, v)
  co <- coef(fit)
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, length(lat), length(lat), dimnames = list(lat, lat))
  for (i in seq_along(lat)) for (j in seq_along(lat))
    out[i, j] <- co[sprintf("m1.S[%d,%d]", min(idx[i], idx[j]), max(idx[i], idx[j]))]
  out
}
```

## Simulate bivariate growth data

- Process 1: 5 time points
- Process 2: 20 time points

```{r}
set.seed(1957)
latent_cor <- matrix(
    c(1, 0, 0.5, 0.3,
      0, 1, -0.1, -0.3,
      0.5, -0.1, 1, 0.2,
      0.3, -0.3, 0.2, 1),
    nrow = 4
)
latent_sd <- c(1, 0.5, 1.5, 0.6)
latent_cov <- diag(latent_sd) %*% latent_cor %*% diag(latent_sd)
latent_mean <- c(-1, 0.5, 0, -0.3)
# Simulate person-specific growth parameters
n_clus <- 100
eta <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_clus, mu = latent_mean, Sigma = latent_cov,
                     empirical = TRUE)
# Time variables (different time scale for the two processes)
n_time1 <- 5
n_time2 <- 20
# Assume complete data for now
time1 <- rep(seq_len(n_time1) - 1, n_clus)
time2 <- rep(seq_len(n_time2) - 1, n_clus)
# Simulate process 1
clus_id1 <- rep(seq_len(n_clus), each = n_time1)
sigma1 <- 1  # error sd
# Simulate error
e1 <- rnorm(clus_id1)
e1 <- e1 - mean(e1)
e1 <- e1 / sd(e1) * sigma1
y1 <- eta[clus_id1, 1] + time1 * eta[clus_id1, 2] + e1
# Simulate process 2
clus_id2 <- rep(seq_len(n_clus), each = n_time2)
sigma2 <- 2  # error sd
# Simulate error
e2 <- rnorm(clus_id2)
e2 <- e2 - mean(e2)
e2 <- e2 / sd(e2) * sigma2
y2 <- eta[clus_id2, 3] + time2 * eta[clus_id2, 4] + e2
```

```{r}
# Empirical Bayes
m1 <- lmer(y1 ~ time1 + (time1 | clus_id1),
           data = data.frame(y1, time1, clus_id1),
           REML = FALSE)
fs_dat1 <- get_fs(m1)
# Empirical Bayes
m2 <- lmer(y2 ~ time2 + (time2 | clus_id2),
           data = data.frame(y2, time2, clus_id2),
           REML = FALSE)
fs_dat2 <- get_fs(m2)
```

`get_fs()` carries each EB score (`fs_u0`, `fs_u1`) alongside its
per-cluster standard error (`fs_u0_se`), implied loadings (`u0_by_fs_u0`, …),
error variances (`ev_fs_u0`) and error covariance (`ecov_fs_u1_fs_u0`):

```{r}
knitr::kable(head(fs_dat1), digits = 3)
```

The stage-2 function reads the measurement columns automatically.
The EB random effects are deviations from the fixed-effect intercept and
slope, rather than estimates of the person's full trajectory coefficients.
The comparisons below concern variances and covariances of those deviations.
To describe average trajectories, use the fixed effects from the stage-1
mixed models; the stage-2 random-effect means are not the generating
intercept and slope means.

## Using EB Without Accounting for Error

```{r}
eb_m1 <- ranef(m1)[[1]]
eb_m2 <- ranef(m2)[[1]]
cor(cbind(eb_m1, eb_m2))
cov(cbind(eb_m1, eb_m2))
```

These are associations among the EB estimates themselves. Shrinkage and
estimation error can make them differ from the associations among the
underlying random effects. We compare them with the population values below.

## 2S-PA

### Process 1

First estimate the random-intercept and random-slope covariance for one
process. `tspa_mx_model()` returns a fitted model, which can be summarized
directly:

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
tspa1_mx_fit <- tspa_mx_model(model = "u0 ~~ u1\nu0 + u1 ~ 1", data = fs_dat1)
# Summarize the results
summary(tspa1_mx_fit)
```

The estimated variances and covariances for $u_0$ and $u_1$ are similar to the ones in the mixed model.

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
print("2S-PA covariance")
lat_cov(tspa1_mx_fit, c("u0", "u1"))
print("lme4 covariance")
as.matrix(VarCorr(m1)$clus_id1)
```

The examples use maximum likelihood (`REML = FALSE`) for the stage-1
mixed models.

<!-- For REML,

$$
K' y = K' X \gamma + K' Z u + K' e,
$$
with K'X = 0. So

$$
K' y = K' Z u + K' e.
$$ -->

### Process 2

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
tspa2_mx_fit <- tspa_mx_model(model = "u0 ~~ u1\nu0 + u1 ~ 1", data = fs_dat2)
# Summarize the results
summary(tspa2_mx_fit)
```

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
print("2S-PA covariance")
lat_cov(tspa2_mx_fit, c("u0", "u1"))
print("lme4 covariance")
as.matrix(VarCorr(m2)$clus_id2)
```

### Combining Processes 1 and 2

The suffixes `_1` and `_2` distinguish the two processes. Both score datasets
contain the same people in the same order, so we combine their columns.
In an application, verify participant alignment before combining scores.

```{r}
colnames(fs_dat1) <- paste0(colnames(fs_dat1), "_1")
colnames(fs_dat2) <- paste0(colnames(fs_dat2), "_2")
fs_dat <- cbind(fs_dat1, fs_dat2)
```

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
# Unstructured model on the four growth-parameter latents. Explicit fsL/fsT
# here: auto-derivation yields one latent set per frame, so the two
# processes' u0/u1 latents must be named apart (u0_1/u0_2, u1_1/u1_2).
cross_load <- matrix(c("u0_by_fs_u0_1", "u0_by_fs_u1_1", NA, NA,
                        "u1_by_fs_u0_1", "u1_by_fs_u1_1", NA, NA,
                        NA, NA, "u0_by_fs_u0_2", "u0_by_fs_u1_2",
                        NA, NA, "u1_by_fs_u0_2", "u1_by_fs_u1_2"), nrow = 4) |>
     `dimnames<-`(list(c("fs_u0_1", "fs_u1_1", "fs_u0_2", "fs_u1_2"),
                       c("u0_1", "u1_1", "u0_2", "u1_2")))
err_cov <- matrix(c("ev_fs_u0_1", "ecov_fs_u1_fs_u0_1", NA, NA,
                    "ecov_fs_u1_fs_u0_1", "ev_fs_u1_1", NA, NA,
                    NA, NA, "ev_fs_u0_2", "ecov_fs_u1_fs_u0_2",
                    NA, NA, "ecov_fs_u1_fs_u0_2", "ev_fs_u1_2"), nrow = 4) |>
     `dimnames<-`(rep(list(c("fs_u0_1", "fs_u1_1", "fs_u0_2", "fs_u1_2")), 2))
tspa3_mx_fit <- tspa_mx_model(
    model = "u0_1 ~~ u1_1 + u0_2 + u1_2\n
             u1_1 ~~ u0_2 + u1_2\n
             u0_2 ~~ u1_2\n
             u0_1 + u1_1 + u0_2 + u1_2 ~ 1",
    data = fs_dat, fsL = cross_load, fsT = err_cov)
# Summarize the results
summary(tspa3_mx_fit)
```

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
lat3 <- c("u0_1", "u1_1", "u0_2", "u1_2")
knitr::kable(cov(cbind(eb_m1, eb_m2)), digits = 3, caption = "EB covariance")
knitr::kable(lat_cov(tspa3_mx_fit, lat3), digits = 3, caption = "2S-PA covariance")
knitr::kable(latent_cov, digits = 3, caption = "Population covariance")
```

The three tables compare covariances of the EB estimates, 2S-PA latent
covariances, and the generating population covariances. In this simulated
sample, measurement-error correction brings the cross-process covariances
closer to the population values. Differences remain because the estimates
are based on only 100 participants. A single simulated sample cannot
establish an estimator's bias; that requires repeated-sampling evaluation.

# With Missing Data

Next, remove some observations, with a higher probability of missingness
at later occasions. Missingness depends on observed time, so this
simulation uses a missing-at-random mechanism conditional on time.

```{r}
set.seed(1942)
# Missing indicators
r1 <- rbinom(time1, size = 1, prob = (20 - time1) / 20 - 0.05)
r2 <- rbinom(time2, size = 1, prob = (100 - time2) / 100 - 0.05)
```

Model with missing data

```{r}
# Empirical Bayes
m1 <- lmer(y1 ~ time1 + (time1 | clus_id1),
           data = data.frame(y1, time1, clus_id1),
           REML = FALSE, subset = r1 == 1)
fs_dat1 <- get_fs(m1)
# Empirical Bayes
m2 <- lmer(y2 ~ time2 + (time2 | clus_id2),
           data = data.frame(y2, time2, clus_id2),
           REML = FALSE, subset = r2 == 1)
fs_dat2 <- get_fs(m2)
colnames(fs_dat1) <- paste0(colnames(fs_dat1), "_1")
colnames(fs_dat2) <- paste0(colnames(fs_dat2), "_2")
fs_dat <- cbind(fs_dat1, fs_dat2)
```

People now differ in both the number and timing of observed occasions.
Their score loadings and error covariances consequently vary:

```{r}
head(fs_dat)
```

Fit the same stage-2 model using the updated measurement information.
The `mxTryHard()` call retries optimization to seek a converged solution:

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
tspa3o_mx <- tspa_mx_model(
    model = "u0_1 ~~ u1_1 + u0_2 + u1_2\n
             u1_1 ~~ u0_2 + u1_2\n
             u0_2 ~~ u1_2\n
             u0_1 + u1_1 + u0_2 + u1_2 ~ 1",
    data = fs_dat, fsL = cross_load, fsT = err_cov)
# Retry optimization
tspa3o_mx_fit <- mxTryHard(tspa3o_mx)
# Summarize the results
summary(tspa3o_mx_fit)
```

```{r, eval = have_openmx}
lat3 <- c("u0_1", "u1_1", "u0_2", "u1_2")
knitr::kable(cov(cbind(fs_dat1[, 1:2], fs_dat2[, 1:2])), digits = 3, caption = "EB covariance")
knitr::kable(lat_cov(tspa3o_mx_fit, lat3), digits = 3, caption = "2S-PA covariance")
knitr::kable(latent_cov, digits = 3, caption = "Population covariance")
```

## Reference

Lai, M. H. C., & Liu, S. (2026). A two-stage approach to account for
measurement error when using empirical Bayes estimates of random slopes.
*Psychological Methods*. Advance online publication.
<https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000838>
